claim: Perceptual learning can induce plasticity in the adult dorsolateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN) of the thalamus in human subjects.
source: However, several recent studies have demonstrated that plasticity also occurs in the adult dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN) of the thalamus of human subjects during perceptual learning (Yu et al., 2016) and mice upon monocular deprivation (MD) (Huh et al., 2020; Jaepel et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yu et al., 2016

claim: Monocular deprivation can induce plasticity in the adult dLGN of mice.
source: However, several recent studies have demonstrated that plasticity also occurs in the adult dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN) of the thalamus of human subjects during perceptual learning (Yu et al., 2016) and mice upon monocular deprivation (MD) (Huh et al., 2020; Jaepel et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Huh et al., 2020 and Jaepel et al., 2017

claim: Neurons preferentially respond to visual stimuli presented to one eye versus the other, a property called ocular dominance (OD).
source: OD is the property that neurons preferentially respond to visual stimuli presented to one eye versus the other (Wiesel and Hubel, 1963a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wiesel and Hubel, 1963a

claim: A period of monocular deprivation results in an OD shift in V1 neurons due to weakened responses to the deprived eye and strengthened responses to the non-deprived eye.
source: Visual experience affects OD and a period of MD results in an OD shift in V1 neurons due to weakened responses to the deprived eye and strengthened responses to the non-deprived eye (Hensch and Stryker, 1996; Wiesel and Hubel, 1963a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hensch and Stryker, 1996 and Wiesel and Hubel, 1963a

claim: OD plasticity is most prominent during a critical period of development.
source: OD plasticity is most prominent during a critical period of development (Gordon and Stryker, 1996; Wiesel and Hubel, 1963a) but can also be induced in young adult mice (Heimel et al., 2007; Hofer et al., 2006; Lehmann and Löwel, 2008; Sato and Stryker, 2008; Sawtell et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gordon and Stryker, 1996 and Wiesel and Hubel, 1963a

claim: OD plasticity can be induced in young adult mice.
source: OD plasticity is most prominent during a critical period of development (Gordon and Stryker, 1996; Wiesel and Hubel, 1963a) but can also be induced in young adult mice (Heimel et al., 2007; Hofer et al., 2006; Lehmann and Löwel, 2008; Sato and Stryker, 2008; Sawtell et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Heimel et al., 2007; Hofer et al., 2006; Lehmann and Löwel, 2008; Sato and Stryker, 2008; Sawtell et al., 2003

claim: Adult OD plasticity requires a longer period of deprivation than critical period OD plasticity.
source: This requires a longer period of deprivation, however, and the shift is smaller and less persistent and is mediated predominantly by strengthening of responses to the non-deprived eye (Frenkel and Bear, 2004; Heimel et al., 2007; Hofer et al., 2006; Lehmann and Löwel, 2008; Sato and Stryker, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Frenkel and Bear, 2004; Heimel et al., 2007; Hofer et al., 2006; Lehmann and Löwel, 2008; Sato and Stryker, 2008

claim: Adult OD plasticity is smaller and less persistent than critical period OD plasticity.
source: This requires a longer period of deprivation, however, and the shift is smaller and less persistent and is mediated predominantly by strengthening of responses to the non-deprived eye (Frenkel and Bear, 2004; Heimel et al., 2007; Hofer et al., 2006; Lehmann and Löwel, 2008; Sato and Stryker, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Frenkel and Bear, 2004; Heimel et al., 2007; Hofer et al., 2006; Lehmann and Löwel, 2008; Sato and Stryker, 2008

claim: Adult OD plasticity is mediated predominantly by strengthening of responses to the non-deprived eye.
source: This requires a longer period of deprivation, however, and the shift is smaller and less persistent and is mediated predominantly by strengthening of responses to the non-deprived eye (Frenkel and Bear, 2004; Heimel et al., 2007; Hofer et al., 2006; Lehmann and Löwel, 2008; Sato and Stryker, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Frenkel and Bear, 2004; Heimel et al., 2007; Hofer et al., 2006; Lehmann and Löwel, 2008; Sato and Stryker, 2008

claim: During the critical period, extensive OD plasticity can be induced in dLGN.
source: Previously, we demonstrated that during the critical period extensive OD plasticity can be induced in dLGN and that this requires synaptic inhibition in the thalamus (Sommeijer et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sommeijer et al., 2017

claim: OD plasticity in dLGN during the critical period requires synaptic inhibition in the thalamus.
source: Previously, we demonstrated that during the critical period extensive OD plasticity can be induced in dLGN and that this requires synaptic inhibition in the thalamus (Sommeijer et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sommeijer et al., 2017

claim: OD plasticity in dLGN is strongly reduced in Gabra1 cKO mice during the critical period.
source: Multielectrode recordings revealed that OD plasticity in dLGN is strongly reduced in mice in which thalamic synaptic inhibition is inactivated by deleting the gene encoding the GABA receptor alpha1 subunit (Gabra1) selectively in the dorsal thalamus (Gabra1fl/fl × Olig3Cre/+ mice, hereafter referred to as 'Gabra1 cKO mice').
evidence: Supported by citation to Sommeijer et al., 2017 in the previous sentence

claim: OD plasticity induced by long-term MD is reduced in V1 of Gabra1 cKO mice during the critical period due to the absence of ipsilateral eye response strengthening.
source: Interestingly, OD plasticity induced by long-term MD is also reduced in V1 of these mice due to the absence of ipsilateral eye response strengthening (Sommeijer et al., 2017), suggesting that during the critical period thalamic plasticity contributes to plasticity in V1.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sommeijer et al., 2017

claim: During the critical period, thalamic plasticity contributes to plasticity in V1.
source: Interestingly, OD plasticity induced by long-term MD is also reduced in V1 of these mice due to the absence of ipsilateral eye response strengthening (Sommeijer et al., 2017), suggesting that during the critical period thalamic plasticity contributes to plasticity in V1.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that OD plasticity is reduced in V1 of Gabra1 cKO mice, supported by citation to Sommeijer et al., 2017

claim: In adult mice lacking thalamic synaptic inhibition, OD plasticity is absent in both dLGN and V1.
source: We find that in adult mice lacking thalamic synaptic inhibition OD plasticity is absent in both dLGN and V1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figures 2 and 3)

claim: Silencing V1 of adult wild-type mice does not affect the OD shift in dLGN.
source: Silencing V1 of adult wild-type (WT) mice does not affect the OD shift in dLGN, showing that it does not depend on feedback from V1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 5C-E)

claim: The OD shift in adult dLGN does not depend on feedback from V1.
source: Silencing V1 of adult wild-type (WT) mice does not affect the OD shift in dLGN, showing that it does not depend on feedback from V1.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that silencing V1 does not affect the OD shift in dLGN, supported by experimental data (Figure 5C-E)

claim: During the critical period, the OD shift in dLGN partially depends on activity in V1.
source: In contrast, we find that during the critical period the OD shift in dLGN partially depends on activity in V1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 5F-H)

claim: Thalamocortical interactions underlying OD plasticity change with age.
source: Together, our findings show that thalamocortical interactions underlying OD plasticity change with age and suggest that the thalamus may be an important source of plasticity in adult learning events that have generally been considered cortical processes.
evidence: Inference based on the differences observed between critical period and adult OD plasticity mechanisms, supported by experimental data

claim: The thalamus may be an important source of plasticity in adult learning events that have generally been considered cortical processes.
source: Together, our findings show that thalamocortical interactions underlying OD plasticity change with age and suggest that the thalamus may be an important source of plasticity in adult learning events that have generally been considered cortical processes.
evidence: Speculation based on the findings that adult V1 plasticity depends on thalamic plasticity

claim: During the critical period, visual responses of dLGN neurons in Gabra1 cKO mice were less sustained due to the lack of thalamic synaptic inhibition.
source: Previous work showed that during the critical period visual responses of dLGN neurons in Gabra1fl/fl × Olig3Cre/+ (Gabra1 cKO) mice were less sustained due to the lack of thalamic synaptic inhibition, while average response strengths and basic receptive field properties seemed surprisingly unaffected (Sommeijer et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sommeijer et al., 2017

claim: During the critical period, average response strengths and basic receptive field properties in dLGN neurons of Gabra1 cKO mice seemed surprisingly unaffected.
source: Previous work showed that during the critical period visual responses of dLGN neurons in Gabra1fl/fl × Olig3Cre/+ (Gabra1 cKO) mice were less sustained due to the lack of thalamic synaptic inhibition, while average response strengths and basic receptive field properties seemed surprisingly unaffected (Sommeijer et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sommeijer et al., 2017

claim: Receptive field sizes in adult dLGN do not differ between Gabra1 cKO and WT mice.
source: We observed no differences in receptive field sizes in Gabra1 cKO and WT mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Receptive field sizes in dLGN become smaller between eye opening and critical period onset.
source: As receptive field sizes in dLGN are known to become smaller between eye opening and critical period onset (Tschetter et al., 2018), this observation suggests that dLGN develops surprisingly normally in the absence of synaptic inhibition.
evidence: Supported by citation to Tschetter et al., 2018

claim: dLGN develops surprisingly normally in the absence of synaptic inhibition.
source: As receptive field sizes in dLGN are known to become smaller between eye opening and critical period onset (Tschetter et al., 2018), this observation suggests that dLGN develops surprisingly normally in the absence of synaptic inhibition.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that receptive field sizes are similar in WT and Gabra1 cKO mice, supported by data in Figure 1C

claim: The numbers, densities, and sizes of inhibitory and cholinergic boutons increase between eye opening and critical period onset.
source: To investigate this further, we analyzed the numbers, densities, and sizes of inhibitory and cholinergic boutons, which are also known to increase during the same developmental window (Bickford et al., 2010; Sommeijer et al., 2017; Sokhadze et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bickford et al., 2010; Sommeijer et al., 2017; Sokhadze et al., 2018

claim: In adult WT and Gabra1 cKO mice, no differences were observed in the numbers, densities, and sizes of inhibitory and cholinergic boutons.
source: Again, in adult WT and Gabra1 cKO mice we observed no differences (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: In WT mice, 51% of recorded dLGN neurons were binocular.
source: In WT mice, 51% of recorded neurons were binocular and in Gabra1 cKO mice 59%.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from single unit recordings

claim: In Gabra1 cKO mice, 59% of recorded dLGN neurons were binocular.
source: In WT mice, 51% of recorded neurons were binocular and in Gabra1 cKO mice 59%.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from single unit recordings

claim: In Gabra1 cKO mice, visual responses attenuated faster than in WT siblings.
source: This revealed that in Gabra1 cKO mice visual responses attenuated faster than in WT siblings: peak responses were stronger, but weaker responses were observed during the phase of prolonged firing (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: In Gabra1 cKO mice, peak responses were stronger than in WT mice.
source: This revealed that in Gabra1 cKO mice visual responses attenuated faster than in WT siblings: peak responses were stronger, but weaker responses were observed during the phase of prolonged firing (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: In Gabra1 cKO mice, weaker responses were observed during the phase of prolonged firing compared to WT mice.
source: This revealed that in Gabra1 cKO mice visual responses attenuated faster than in WT siblings: peak responses were stronger, but weaker responses were observed during the phase of prolonged firing (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: The attenuation index was increased in Gabra1 cKO mice compared to WT mice.
source: Thus, while average response strength in Gabra1 cKO mice was similar to that in WT mice, the attenuation index was increased.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Average response strength in Gabra1 cKO mice was similar to that in WT mice.
source: Thus, while average response strength in Gabra1 cKO mice was similar to that in WT mice, the attenuation index was increased.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Visual responses in dLGN neurons in adult Gabra1 cKO and WT mice mostly differ in their temporal profile.
source: These results show that like the situation during the critical period (Sommeijer et al., 2017) visual responses in dLGN neurons in adult Gabra1 cKO and WT mice mostly differ in their temporal profile, while average response strengths and receptive fields sizes are hardly changed.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1 and citation to Sommeijer et al., 2017

claim: Average response strengths and receptive field sizes in dLGN neurons are hardly changed between adult Gabra1 cKO and WT mice.
source: These results show that like the situation during the critical period (Sommeijer et al., 2017) visual responses in dLGN neurons in adult Gabra1 cKO and WT mice mostly differ in their temporal profile, while average response strengths and receptive fields sizes are hardly changed.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1

claim: After 1 week of MD, a significant OD shift occurred in dLGN of adult WT mice.
source: We found that after 1 wk of MD a significant OD shift occurred in dLGN of adult WT mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The OD shift in adult WT dLGN was predominantly caused by a significant increase in the responses to the non-deprived ipsilateral eye.
source: This was predominantly caused by a significant increase in the responses to the non-deprived ipsilateral eye (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: In Gabra1 cKO mice, no OD shift could be induced in dLGN after 1 week of MD.
source: In Gabra1 cKO mice, no OD shift could be induced in dLGN (Figure 2B) and no significant changes were observed in the responses to the ipsi- or contralateral eye (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2D

claim: In Gabra1 cKO mice, no significant changes were observed in the responses to the ipsi- or contralateral eye after 1 week of MD.
source: In Gabra1 cKO mice, no OD shift could be induced in dLGN (Figure 2B) and no significant changes were observed in the responses to the ipsi- or contralateral eye (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: In adulthood, OD plasticity in dLGN depends on thalamic synaptic inhibition.
source: Together, these results show that also in adulthood OD plasticity in dLGN depends on thalamic synaptic inhibition.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that OD plasticity is absent in Gabra1 cKO mice lacking thalamic synaptic inhibition, supported by data in Figure 2

claim: During the critical period, brief MD induces a normal OD shift in V1 of Gabra1 cKO mice.
source: Brief MD induces a normal OD shift, but longer MD does not cause the OD shift to strengthen further (Sommeijer et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sommeijer et al., 2017

claim: During the critical period, longer MD does not cause the OD shift to strengthen further in V1 of Gabra1 cKO mice.
source: Brief MD induces a normal OD shift, but longer MD does not cause the OD shift to strengthen further (Sommeijer et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sommeijer et al., 2017

claim: The critical period opens normally in V1 of Gabra1 cKO mice.
source: This suggests that the critical period opens normally in V1 of Gabra1 cKO mice, but that the second, homeostatic phase of the OD shift depends on thalamic inhibition and plasticity.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that brief MD induces a normal OD shift in Gabra1 cKO mice, supported by citation to Sommeijer et al., 2017

claim: The second, homeostatic phase of the OD shift during the critical period depends on thalamic inhibition and plasticity.
source: This suggests that the critical period opens normally in V1 of Gabra1 cKO mice, but that the second, homeostatic phase of the OD shift depends on thalamic inhibition and plasticity.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that longer MD does not strengthen the OD shift in Gabra1 cKO mice, supported by citation to Sommeijer et al., 2017

claim: Residual OD plasticity in adult V1 has various similarities with the second phase of OD plasticity during the critical period.
source: Residual OD plasticity in adult V1 has various similarities with the second phase of OD plasticity during the critical period and also requires long-term MD.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about OD plasticity

claim: Residual OD plasticity in adult V1 requires long-term MD.
source: Residual OD plasticity in adult V1 has various similarities with the second phase of OD plasticity during the critical period and also requires long-term MD.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about OD plasticity

claim: Receptive field sizes in V1 did not differ between Gabra1 cKO and WT mice.
source: Like in dLGN, receptive field sizes did not differ between Gabra1 cKO and WT mice and were not affected by a week of MD (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Receptive field sizes in V1 were not affected by a week of MD.
source: Like in dLGN, receptive field sizes did not differ between Gabra1 cKO and WT mice and were not affected by a week of MD (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Visual responses in V1 were more attenuated in Gabra1 cKO mice than in WT mice.
source: Like in dLGN, visual responses in V1 were more attenuated in Gabra1 cKO mice than in WT mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: A clear OD shift was induced in V1 of monocularly deprived WT mice after 7 days of MD.
source: A clear OD shift was induced in V1 of monocularly deprived WT mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E

claim: The OD shift in V1 of adult WT mice involved an increase in open, ipsilateral eye responses.
source: As expected, the OD shift involved an increase in open, ipsilateral eye responses (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F

claim: A significant decrease of deprived, contralateral eye responses was found in V1 of adult WT mice after 7 days of MD.
source: We also found a significant decrease of deprived, contralateral eye responses (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F

claim: Several studies have provided evidence that a loss of contralateral eye responses contributes less to adult OD plasticity than during the critical period.
source: While several studies have provided evidence that a loss of contralateral eye responses contributes less to adult OD plasticity than during the critical period (Frenkel and Bear, 2004; Kalogeraki et al., 2017; Sato and Stryker, 2008), others have shown that it still occurs in adulthood (Rose et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Frenkel and Bear, 2004; Kalogeraki et al., 2017; Sato and Stryker, 2008

claim: Loss of contralateral eye responses still occurs in adulthood.
source: While several studies have provided evidence that a loss of contralateral eye responses contributes less to adult OD plasticity than during the critical period (Frenkel and Bear, 2004; Kalogeraki et al., 2017; Sato and Stryker, 2008), others have shown that it still occurs in adulthood (Rose et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rose et al., 2016

claim: The OD shift after 7 days of MD was negligible in adult Gabra1 cKO mice.
source: In adult Gabra1 cKO mice, the OD shift after 7 d of MD was negligible and significantly smaller than in WT mice (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and 3G

claim: The OD shift after 7 days of MD was significantly smaller in adult Gabra1 cKO mice than in WT mice.
source: In adult Gabra1 cKO mice, the OD shift after 7 d of MD was negligible and significantly smaller than in WT mice (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E

claim: The contra- and ipsilateral eye responses in V1 of non-deprived Gabra1 cKO mice were of comparable strength as those observed in WT mice.
source: The contra- and ipsilateral eye responses in V1 of non-deprived Gabra1 cKO mice were of comparable strength as those observed in WT mice, despite the lack of synaptic inhibition in the thalamus.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and 3G

claim: After 7 days of MD, no significant strengthening of ipsilateral eye responses occurred in V1 of Gabra1 cKO mice.
source: After 7 d of MD, no significant strengthening of ipsilateral eye responses or weakening of deprived eye responses occurred (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G

claim: After 7 days of MD, no significant weakening of deprived eye responses occurred in V1 of Gabra1 cKO mice.
source: After 7 d of MD, no significant strengthening of ipsilateral eye responses or weakening of deprived eye responses occurred (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G

claim: In adult mice, absence of synaptic inhibition in the thalamus reduces OD plasticity in V1.
source: We conclude that in adult mice absence of synaptic inhibition in the thalamus reduces OD plasticity in V1.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that OD plasticity is absent in V1 of Gabra1 cKO mice, supported by data in Figure 3

claim: dLGN relay cells are strongly innervated by excitatory feedback connections from layer 6 cells in V1.
source: Apart from the retinal input dLGN relay cells receive, they are also strongly innervated by excitatory feedback connections from layer 6 cells in V1.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about thalamocortical circuits

claim: dLGN neurons receive bisynaptic inhibitory feedback from V1 via the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) and local interneurons.
source: Additionally, dLGN neurons receive bisynaptic inhibitory feedback from V1 via the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) and local interneurons (Figure 4A).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about thalamocortical circuits, illustrated in Figure 4A

claim: Responses of dLGN relay cells to the ipsi- or contralateral eye may be strengthened or inhibited by V1 feedback depending on whether excitatory or inhibitory feedback dominates.
source: Depending on whether excitatory or inhibitory feedback dominates, responses of dLGN relay cells to the ipsi- or contralateral eye in dLGN may be strengthened or inhibited by V1 feedback (Denman and Contreras, 2015; Howarth et al., 2014; Jaepel et al., 2017; Kirchgessner et al., 2020; Olsen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Denman and Contreras, 2015; Howarth et al., 2014; Jaepel et al., 2017; Kirchgessner et al., 2020; Olsen et al., 2012

claim: Feedback inputs from V1 can influence the OD of relay cells in dLGN.
source: These feedback inputs from V1 can thus influence the OD of relay cells in dLGN.
evidence: Inference based on the fact that V1 feedback can strengthen or inhibit dLGN responses

claim: Muscimol injections effectively silenced V1.
source: Muscimol injections effectively silenced V1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Silencing V1 did not alter responses to the contra- or ipsilateral eye in individual units in dLGN of adult WT mice on average.
source: On average, silencing V1 did not alter responses to the contra- or ipsilateral eye in individual units in dLGN of adult WT mice (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B-D

claim: In Gabra1 cKO mice, V1 silencing did not significantly affect responses to the contralateral eye in dLGN.
source: In Gabra1 cKO mice, V1 silencing also did not significantly affect responses to the contralateral eye (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-G

claim: In Gabra1 cKO mice, responses to the ipsilateral eye showed a trend towards weakening after silencing V1, but this did not reach significance.
source: Responses to the ipsilateral eye showed a trend towards weakening after silencing V1, but this did not reach significance (p=0.094).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G

claim: In the absence of synaptic inhibition in the thalamus, V1 feedback has relatively little influence on dLGN responses to the contra- or ipsilateral eye.
source: Thus, also in the absence of synaptic inhibition in the thalamus, V1 feedback has relatively little influence on dLGN responses to the contra- or ipsilateral eye.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that V1 silencing does not significantly affect dLGN responses in Gabra1 cKO mice, supported by data in Figure 4

claim: The ODI in non-deprived WT mice did not change after silencing V1.
source: In non-deprived mice, the ODI did not change after silencing V1 of WT mice (Figure 5A), as expected considering that contra- and ipsilateral eye response strengths were not affected by V1 feedback (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The ODI in non-deprived Gabra1 cKO mice did not change upon silencing V1.
source: Similarly, the ODI in non-deprived Gabra1 cKO mice did not change upon silencing V1 (Figure 5B), which was also expected based on the small changes in contra- and lateral eye responses that we observed (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Silencing V1 did not affect the OD measured in dLGN of adult monocularly deprived WT mice.
source: Despite the considerable OD shift we observed in V1 of adult WT mice, silencing V1 did not affect the OD measured in dLGN (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Average responses to the two eyes in dLGN of adult monocularly deprived WT mice were not altered in the absence of cortical feedback.
source: Also, average responses to the two eyes were not altered in the absence of cortical feedback (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and E

claim: The OD shift in adult dLGN is not inherited from V1.
source: This confirms that the OD shift in adult dLGN is not inherited from V1 (Jaepel et al., 2017) and supports the idea that dLGN plasticity involves the plasticity of retinogeniculate afferents.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that silencing V1 does not affect the OD shift in dLGN, supported by data in Figure 5C-E and citation to Jaepel et al., 2017

claim: dLGN plasticity involves the plasticity of retinogeniculate afferents.
source: This confirms that the OD shift in adult dLGN is not inherited from V1 (Jaepel et al., 2017) and supports the idea that dLGN plasticity involves the plasticity of retinogeniculate afferents.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that the OD shift in dLGN is not inherited from V1, supported by data in Figure 5C-E

claim: During the critical period, silencing V1 did not affect ipsi- or contralateral eye responses in non-deprived WT mice.
source: Interestingly, when we repeated this experiment in (C57Bl/6JRj) WT mice during the critical period, we found that silencing V1 also did not affect ipsi- or contralateral eye responses in non-deprived mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), but selectively reduced ipsilateral eye responses in monocularly deprived mice (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: During the critical period, silencing V1 selectively reduced ipsilateral eye responses in monocularly deprived WT mice.
source: Interestingly, when we repeated this experiment in (C57Bl/6JRj) WT mice during the critical period, we found that silencing V1 also did not affect ipsi- or contralateral eye responses in non-deprived mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), but selectively reduced ipsilateral eye responses in monocularly deprived mice (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G and H

claim: During the critical period, silencing V1 significantly reduced the OD shift in monocularly deprived WT mice.
source: Consequently, silencing V1 significantly reduced the OD shift in these animals (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F

claim: The change in ODI caused by V1 silencing in mice during the critical period was significantly larger than that in adult WT.
source: The change in ODI caused by V1 silencing in mice during the critical period was significantly larger than that in adult WT (p=0.034).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of experimental data

claim: During the critical period, corticothalamic connections strengthen the OD shift in dLGN.
source: Thus, during the critical period, corticothalamic connections strengthen the OD shift in dLGN, while they do not in adulthood.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that V1 silencing reduces the OD shift in dLGN during the critical period but not in adulthood, supported by data in Figure 5

claim: In adulthood, corticothalamic connections do not strengthen the OD shift in dLGN.
source: Thus, during the critical period, corticothalamic connections strengthen the OD shift in dLGN, while they do not in adulthood.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that V1 silencing does not affect the OD shift in dLGN in adulthood, supported by data in Figure 5C-E

claim: In monocularly deprived adult Gabra1 cKO mice, silencing V1 did not affect responses to the contralateral eye in dLGN.
source: In monocularly deprived adult Gabra1 cKO mice (Figure 5I–K), silencing V1 did not affect responses to the contralateral eye, but significantly reduced those to the ipsilateral eye (Figure 5J and K), similarly to what we observed in WT mice during the critical period.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J

claim: In monocularly deprived adult Gabra1 cKO mice, silencing V1 significantly reduced responses to the ipsilateral eye in dLGN.
source: In monocularly deprived adult Gabra1 cKO mice (Figure 5I–K), silencing V1 did not affect responses to the contralateral eye, but significantly reduced those to the ipsilateral eye (Figure 5J and K), similarly to what we observed in WT mice during the critical period.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5K

claim: The average ODI in monocularly deprived Gabra1 cKO mice was not significantly altered by V1 silencing.
source: However, despite this effect of V1 silencing, the average ODI in monocularly deprived Gabra1 cKO mice was not significantly altered by it (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I

claim: Feedback from V1 does not affect OD in the dLGN of adult mice, independently of whether they are monocularly deprived or lack synaptic inhibition in the thalamus.
source: We conclude that feedback from V1 does not affect OD in the dLGN of adult mice, independently of whether they are monocularly deprived or lack synaptic inhibition in the thalamus.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that V1 silencing does not significantly affect ODI in adult mice, supported by data in Figure 5

claim: During the critical period, V1 silencing reduces the OD shift observed in dLGN.
source: During the critical period, however, V1 silencing does reduce the OD shift observed in dLGN.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F-H

claim: In dLGN of adult mice, 7 days of MD causes a strong OD shift.
source: In line with previous work (Jaepel et al., 2017), we find that in dLGN of adult mice, 7 d of MD causes a strong OD shift.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and citation to Jaepel et al., 2017

claim: The main substrate of plasticity in adult dLGN appears to be the retinogeniculate synapse.
source: The main substrate of this plasticity in adult dLGN appears to be the retinogeniculate synapse as silencing V1, the other main source of visual input to dLGN, does not affect the OD shift.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that silencing V1 does not affect the OD shift in dLGN, supported by data in Figure 5C-E

claim: Many relay cells in dLGN receive binocular inputs.
source: Recent work has shown that while many relay cells in dLGN receive binocular inputs (Rompani et al., 2017), synapses from the non-dominant eye are often silent and dominated by NMDA receptors (Bauer et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rompani et al., 2017

claim: Synapses from the non-dominant eye in dLGN relay cells are often silent and dominated by NMDA receptors.
source: Recent work has shown that while many relay cells in dLGN receive binocular inputs (Rompani et al., 2017), synapses from the non-dominant eye are often silent and dominated by NMDA receptors (Bauer et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bauer et al., 2021

claim: Silent synapses contribute strongly to OD plasticity in V1.
source: Because silent synapses contribute strongly to OD plasticity in V1, it is interesting to speculate that OD plasticity in dLGN also involves the unsilencing and strengthening of these synapses (Huang et al., 2015; Yusifov et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Huang et al., 2015; Yusifov et al., 2021

claim: OD plasticity in dLGN may involve the unsilencing and strengthening of silent synapses.
source: Because silent synapses contribute strongly to OD plasticity in V1, it is interesting to speculate that OD plasticity in dLGN also involves the unsilencing and strengthening of these synapses (Huang et al., 2015; Yusifov et al., 2021).
evidence: Speculation based on the role of silent synapses in V1 plasticity, supported by citations to Huang et al., 2015; Yusifov et al., 2021

claim: The OD shift in adult mice involves many monocular contralateral eye-selective neurons becoming binocular.
source: Indeed, the OD shift in adult mice involves many (monocular) contralateral eye-selective neurons to become binocular (Jaepel et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jaepel et al., 2017

claim: A recent study did not observe an OD shift in dLGN of adult mice upon 6 days of MD.
source: In apparent contradiction to our findings and the work by Jaepel et al., a recent study (Li et al., 2023) did not observe an OD shift in dLGN of adult mice upon 6 d of MD.
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2023

claim: Li et al. only included binocular dLGN neurons in their analysis.
source: A possible explanation for this apparent discrepancy is that Li et al. only included binocular dLGN neurons in the analysis.
evidence: Inference based on methodological differences between studies

claim: Including only binocular dLGN neurons in the analysis will exclude monocular, contralateral-eye selective neurons from non-deprived animals, thus decreasing the measured OD shift.
source: This approach will exclude the monocular, contralateral-eye selective neurons in non-deprived animals from the analysis, thus decreasing the measured OD shift.
evidence: Inference based on methodological considerations

claim: In GAD65-deficient mice, reduced GABA release interferes with the onset of the critical period of cortical OD plasticity.
source: However, we did not find evidence for halted thalamic development. Receptive fields of dLGN relay cells become smaller between eye opening and critical period onset (Tschetter et al., 2018), and we find that in WT and Gabra1 cKO mice receptive field sizes are the same.
evidence: Supported by citation to Fagiolini and Hensch, 2000 in the previous sentence

claim: The primary difference between WT and Gabra1 cKO mice in adult dLGN appears to be the lack of synaptic inhibition.
source: The primary difference between WT and Gabra1 cKO mice in adult dLGN thus appears to be the lack of synaptic inhibition.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that other developmental markers are similar between WT and Gabra1 cKO mice

claim: The lack of synaptic inhibition in adult dLGN may interfere with OD plasticity through altered temporal profile of visual responses, which could interfere with spike timing-dependent plasticity.
source: We do not know how this lack of synaptic inhibition in adult dLGN interferes with OD plasticity, but a possible explanation may lie in altered temporal profile of the visual responses it causes, which could interfere with spike timing-dependent plasticity.
evidence: Speculation about the mechanism by which lack of synaptic inhibition interferes with OD plasticity

claim: Brief MD induces an OD shift in V1 of Gabra1 cKO mice.
source: We have previously shown that brief MD induces an OD shift in V1 of these mice (Sommeijer et al., 2017), suggesting that the critical period starts normally in Gabra1 cKO mice.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sommeijer et al., 2017

claim: The critical period starts normally in Gabra1 cKO mice.
source: We have previously shown that brief MD induces an OD shift in V1 of these mice (Sommeijer et al., 2017), suggesting that the critical period starts normally in Gabra1 cKO mice.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that brief MD induces an OD shift in V1 of Gabra1 cKO mice, supported by citation to Sommeijer et al., 2017

claim: Both during the critical period and in adulthood, the late phase of OD plasticity in V1 induced by long-term MD requires thalamic plasticity or inhibition.
source: It thus appears that both during the critical period and in adulthood, the late phase of OD plasticity in V1 induced by long-term MD requires thalamic plasticity or inhibition.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that long-term MD does not induce OD plasticity in V1 of Gabra1 cKO mice during both the critical period and adulthood

claim: MD-induced changes in dLGN relay cell responses to inputs from the two eyes contribute to the OD shift in V1.
source: The most straightforward explanation for the cortical plasticity deficit is that MD-induced changes in dLGN relay cell responses to inputs from the two eyes contribute to the OD shift in V1.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that OD plasticity in V1 is absent when thalamic plasticity is absent

claim: The strengthening of responses to the non-deprived eye in dLGN neurons may provide their axons with a competitive advantage during OD plasticity in V1.
source: Additionally, the strengthening of responses to the non-deprived eye in dLGN neurons may provide their axons with a competitive advantage during OD plasticity in V1, further enhancing the OD shift in V1.
evidence: Speculation about the mechanism by which thalamic plasticity contributes to cortical plasticity

claim: OD plasticity in V1 may be affected by deficits in spike timing-dependent plasticity due to the more attenuated nature of dLGN responses in Gabra1 cKO mice.
source: Finally, it possible that OD plasticity in V1 is also affected by deficits in spike timing-dependent plasticity due to the more attenuated nature of dLGN responses that we observe in Gabra1 cKO mice.
evidence: Speculation about an additional mechanism by which lack of thalamic inhibition may affect V1 plasticity

claim: Thalamic inhibition and plasticity play a crucial role in OD plasticity in adult V1.
source: Together, our results indicate that thalamic inhibition and plasticity play a crucial role in OD plasticity in adult V1, regardless of a possible developmental contribution to the plasticity deficit in dLGN.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that OD plasticity in adult V1 is absent in Gabra1 cKO mice, supported by data in Figure 3

claim: Binocularity in mouse dLGN may be lower than suggested by multi-electrode recordings.
source: The study by Bauer et al., 2021 showed that binocularity in mouse dLGN may be lower than suggested by the current study and earlier work (Howarth et al., 2014; Li et al., 2023; Sommeijer et al., 2017) that involved multi-electrode recordings in dLGN.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bauer et al., 2021

claim: Studies employing electrophysiological recording in dLGN targeted the frontal ipsilateral projection zone of dLGN, which is its most binocular region.
source: Although this difference may be caused by technical limitations of single-unit recordings or calcium imaging, we think it is most likely explained by the fact that studies employing electrophysiological recording in dLGN targeted the frontal ipsilateral projection zone of dLGN, which is its most binocular region (Bauer et al., 2021).
evidence: Inference based on methodological considerations, supported by citation to Bauer et al., 2021

claim: Recording in the frontal ipsilateral projection zone of dLGN will strongly bias towards binocularly responding relay cells.
source: Recording in this region is essential when studying OD plasticity or binocularity in dLGN, but will strongly bias towards binocularly responding relay cells.
evidence: Inference based on methodological considerations

claim: Upon MD or squint during the critical period in cats, the layers responding to the affected eye were thinner.
source: Studies in cats consistently found that upon MD or squint during the critical period the layers responding to the affected eye were thinner (Hickey et al., 1977; Wiesel and Hubel, 1963b) and that the neuronal responses in these layers were slower or weaker (Eysel et al., 1979; Ikeda and Wright, 1976; Sestokas and Lehmkuhle, 1986; Wiesel and Hubel, 1963b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hickey et al., 1977; Wiesel and Hubel, 1963b

claim: Upon MD or squint during the critical period in cats, the neuronal responses in the layers responding to the affected eye were slower or weaker.
source: Studies in cats consistently found that upon MD or squint during the critical period the layers responding to the affected eye were thinner (Hickey et al., 1977; Wiesel and Hubel, 1963b) and that the neuronal responses in these layers were slower or weaker (Eysel et al., 1979; Ikeda and Wright, 1976; Sestokas and Lehmkuhle, 1986; Wiesel and Hubel, 1963b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eysel et al., 1979; Ikeda and Wright, 1976; Sestokas and Lehmkuhle, 1986; Wiesel and Hubel, 1963b

claim: In human amblyopes, dLGN responses to the amblyopic eye were weaker.
source: Also in human amblyopes it was noted that dLGN responses to the amblyopic eye were weaker (Hess et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hess et al., 2009

claim: In human subjects who suffered from glaucoma, the dLGN layers representing the affected eye were thinner.
source: So far, studies on dLGN plasticity by prolonged visual deprivation in adulthood are missing, though it was noted that in human subjects who suffered from glaucoma, the dLGN layers representing the affected eye were thinner (Yücel et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yücel et al., 2001

claim: Inactivation of the nogo-66 receptor in thalamus allows recovery of reduced acuity in adult mice that were monocularly deprived during development.
source: That enhancement of thalamic plasticity is in principle possible is shown by experiments in mice, demonstrating that inactivation of the nogo-66 receptor in thalamus allows recovery of reduced acuity in adult mice that were monocularly deprived during development (Stephany et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stephany et al., 2018

claim: Feedback from V1 does not affect the average strength of response to ipsi- or contralateral eye stimulation in dLGN of adult mice.
source: Despite extensive monosynaptic excitatory feedback and bisynaptic inhibitory feedback (through TRN) from V1, we found that feedback does not affect the average strength of response to ipsi- or contralateral eye stimulation and thus neither the measured OD shift in dLGN of adult mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and 5

claim: The absence of V1 feedback on the OD shift in adult mice was reported previously.
source: The absence of V1 on the OD shift in adult mice was also reported previously (Jaepel et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jaepel et al., 2017

claim: In a previous study, silencing V1 with muscimol reduced the imaged calcium responses in boutons of dLGN axons projecting to V1.
source: However in that study, silencing V1 with muscimol reduced the imaged calcium responses in boutons of dLGN axons projecting to V1, suggesting that dLGN neurons became less responsive to inputs from both eyes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jaepel et al., 2017 in the previous sentence

claim: Muscimol may have a direct effect on thalamocortical inputs, which may reduce calcium responses in synaptic boutons of dLGN neurons without actually reducing their spiking activity at the soma.
source: A possible explanation for this apparent discrepancy may be that muscimol also has a direct effect on thalamocortical inputs (Liu et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2019; Yamauchi et al., 2000), which may reduce calcium responses in synaptic boutons of dLGN neurons without actually reducing their spiking activity at the soma.
evidence: Speculation based on citations to Liu et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2019; Yamauchi et al., 2000

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of layer 6 neurons suppresses dLGN responses.
source: Studies involving optogenetic stimulation of layer 6 neurons find that feedback from V1 suppresses dLGN responses (Denman and Contreras, 2015; Kirchgessner et al., 2020; Olsen et al., 2012), though this differs per cell and changes with stimulus strength and frequency (Kirchgessner et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Denman and Contreras, 2015; Kirchgessner et al., 2020; Olsen et al., 2012

claim: The suppression of dLGN responses by optogenetic stimulation of layer 6 neurons differs per cell and changes with stimulus strength and frequency.
source: Studies involving optogenetic stimulation of layer 6 neurons find that feedback from V1 suppresses dLGN responses (Denman and Contreras, 2015; Kirchgessner et al., 2020; Olsen et al., 2012), though this differs per cell and changes with stimulus strength and frequency (Kirchgessner et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kirchgessner et al., 2020

claim: When V1 feedback is silenced, the average strength of dLGN responses is not reduced in most studies.
source: When V1 feedback is silenced, however, the average strength of dLGN responses is not reduced in most studies (Denman and Contreras, 2015; Howarth et al., 2014; Kirchgessner et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Denman and Contreras, 2015; Howarth et al., 2014; Kirchgessner et al., 2020

claim: Broad optogenetic stimulation of layer 6 predominantly recruits inhibitory feedback, while visual stimulation provides either more balanced or more limited excitatory and inhibitory feedback to dLGN.
source: This suggests that broad optogenetic stimulation of layer 6 predominantly recruits inhibitory feedback, while visual stimulation provides either more balanced or more limited excitatory and inhibitory feedback to dLGN.
evidence: Inference based on the difference between optogenetic stimulation and V1 silencing effects

claim: V1 feedback affects dLGN responses to the ipsilateral eye more strongly than those to the contralateral eye.
source: This suggests that V1 feedback affects dLGN responses to the ipsilateral eye more strongly than those to the contralateral eye.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that V1 silencing affects ipsilateral eye responses more than contralateral eye responses in Gabra1 cKO mice

claim: V1 receives input from the ipsilateral eye through dLGN and also through callosal V1 inputs.
source: This may be the result of V1 receiving input from the ipsilateral eye through dLGN but also through callosal V1 inputs (Cerri et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cerri et al., 2010

claim: Inhibitory innervation of dLGN may be weaker during the critical period than in adulthood.
source: It is possible that inhibitory innervation of dLGN is still weaker during the critical period than in adulthood, causing excitatory feedback from V1 to dominate like in Gabra1 cKO mice.
evidence: Speculation about the mechanism underlying the difference in V1 feedback effects between critical period and adulthood

claim: A stronger OD shift occurs in V1 during the critical period than in adulthood.
source: Additionally, a stronger OD shift occurs in V1 during the critical period, adding to the strength of the cortical feedback representing the ipsilateral eye.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about OD plasticity

claim: An excitotoxic lesion of V1 alters OD in dLGN during development and affects OD plasticity in dLGN at various ages.
source: Interestingly, an excitotoxic lesion of V1 was found to alter OD in dLGN during development and affect OD plasticity in dLGN at various ages (Li et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2023

claim: Continuous crosstalk between thalamus and cortex during development guides plasticity, possibly optimizing thalamocortical and corticothalamic connections.
source: This suggests that continuous crosstalk between thalamus and cortex during development guides plasticity, possibly optimizing thalamocortical and corticothalamic connections.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that excitotoxic lesion of V1 affects dLGN plasticity, supported by citation to Li et al., 2023

claim: The continued absence of corticothalamic feedback is likely to have a much larger impact on dLGN plasticity than acute silencing.
source: The continued absence of corticothalamic feedback is likely to have a much larger impact on dLGN plasticity than the acute silencing we performed.
evidence: Inference based on the difference between chronic lesion and acute silencing

claim: During the critical period, an experience-dependent phase of retinogeniculate refinement takes place, probably optimizing direction-selective inputs from the retina.
source: During the critical period, an experience-dependent phase of retinogeniculate refinement takes place, probably optimizing direction-selective inputs from the retina (Hooks and Chen, 2020; Rompani et al., 2017; Thompson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hooks and Chen, 2020; Rompani et al., 2017; Thompson et al., 2017

claim: Experience-dependent refinement in dLGN during the critical period depends on feedback from V1.
source: This experience-dependent refinement, like OD plasticity in dLGN, also depends on feedback from V1 (Thompson et al., 2017; Thompson et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Thompson et al., 2017; Thompson et al., 2016

claim: Refinement of binocular inputs and direction-selective inputs in dLGN may be one and the same process.
source: It is thus possible that refinement of binocular inputs and direction-selective inputs in dLGN are one and the same process.
evidence: Speculation based on the observation that both processes depend on V1 feedback during the critical period

claim: dLGN retains a high level of plasticity in adulthood.
source: We conclude that dLGN retains a high level of plasticity in adulthood and has considerable influence on cortical plasticity.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that OD plasticity occurs in adult dLGN and affects V1 plasticity, supported by data in Figures 2 and 3

claim: dLGN has considerable influence on cortical plasticity in adulthood.
source: We conclude that dLGN retains a high level of plasticity in adulthood and has considerable influence on cortical plasticity.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that V1 plasticity is absent when thalamic plasticity is absent, supported by data in Figure 3

claim: Thalamic plasticity may be relevant for perceptual learning.
source: This plasticity may not be restricted to binocular responses, but could also be relevant for other forms of perceptual learning (Yu et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculation based on the findings, supported by citation to Yu et al., 2016

claim: A thalamic involvement needs to be considered in amblyopia and learning disabilities.
source: The findings stress that a thalamic involvement needs to be considered in amblyopia and learning disabilities.
evidence: Inference based on the findings that thalamic plasticity affects cortical plasticity

claim: The results may help understanding brain disorders that involve dysfunctional thalamocortical circuits, ranging from attention-deficit disorder to schizophrenia.
source: Additionally, the results may help understanding brain disorders that are thought to involve dysfunctional thalamocortical circuits, ranging from attention-deficit disorder (Wells et al., 2016) to schizophrenia (Benoit et al., 2022; Pinault, 2011; Pratt et al., 2017).
evidence: Speculation based on the findings, supported by citations to Wells et al., 2016; Benoit et al., 2022; Pinault, 2011; Pratt et al., 2017
